text: At every step of the loop, Claude has to pick which tool actually matches the current sub-goal. With two or three tools that's easy. With twenty, several of which sound similar, it isn't — and every tool definition costs tokens on every request, so a disorganized set is both less accurate and more expensive.

Lesson 6's practices are the cheapest layer of routing. Consolidation removes near-duplicate tools before they compete for the same intent. Namespacing keeps tools from different domains from ever looking alike. Precise descriptions resolve what's left between tools that are genuinely similar but not identical.

Sometimes a real system has hundreds or thousands of tools — more than any request should carry up front. Anthropic's own answer is the tool search tool: Claude discovers and loads relevant tools on demand for the current task, instead of seeing the entire catalog on every single request.

The same idea works by hand: a lightweight classification step narrows a large catalog down to a plausible handful before the main agent call even sees the full tool array. Fewer plausible options on the table makes the final selection a much easier choice.

Consolidating near-duplicate tools isn't just convenience — it's a routing fix, removing competition for the same intent before it can happen. Next up: what changes once an agent is actually calling several different tools across one task.
